extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of humor (writers, critics, comedians, literary scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic, prescriptive discussion of what produces humor and how jokes work — intended as theory for writers, comedians, and critics. The chapter articulates psychological, social, and formal conditions that make humorous effects succeed or fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play-attitude (humor arises from play)
rubrics_metrics.description: Play is the preliminary or divertive surface-life in which success is fun, but failure funny; Rabelaisian 'play-attitude' is the native atmosphere of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor is rooted in a playful stance toward life rather than intense seriousness. Works or performers that sustain a play-attitude invite the audience to treat events as playful, making failures comic rather than tragic. Contrast comedy (playful drama) with intense drama where passions are seriously engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as defensive/self-protective instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor functions as a 'little shock-absorber' — an instinct for making the best of a bad thing, protecting us against continual petty disappointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use humor to mitigate irritation and preserve morale: it enables experimentation and persistence. Example: the capacity to smile after a minor physical failure (driving thumb into carpet instead of tack). As a creative principle, humor can reframe losses as tolerable or even enjoyable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of an element of pain or failure
rubrics_metrics.description: In every genuine humorous laugh there is an element which, if sensitivity were exaggerated, would contain the possibility of tears; the laugher has suffered or failed of something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective humor often balances pleasure with an underlying trace of sorrow or disappointment. This bittersweet quality can deepen comic response; avoid purely frivolous 'laughs' if the aim is true humorous resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as philosophic recognition (indifference of pleasure and pain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor recognizes that pleasure and pain are, except for preservation, indifferent — failure is as interesting as success; the humorous sense counsels not taking discriminations too seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a tone of skeptical, flexible appraisal rather than moral absolutism. Humor that relativizes values or mocks pretenses often stems from this philosophical stance; it differs from religion's magnification of seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'point' of a joke — coincidence of negative and positive
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke is a little node or gem-like moment created by the exact coincidence of a playful shock/disappointment (negative current) with a playful or genuine satisfaction (positive current); 'the loss is gain'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct jokes so that an expected loss or balk coincides with an unexpected gratification or aptness. The 'point' is the single instant of coidentity that produces the particular feeling of aptness. Example: the 'Stop counting — it's me!' gag turns anticipated riot into anti-climax + surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor involves two currents — negative and positive
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor (like electricity) possesses two currents: a negative current (a discommoding or thwarting of an aroused interest) and a positive current (a gratification of some interest assumed or aroused).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful jokes require both currents working together. In composing or evaluating a joke, identify the thwarted expectation and the compensatory gratification and ensure they interplay. Failure on either side weakens the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to arouse and proportion audience interest correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke may fail because it does not arouse any interest in the first place, arouses an overly serious interest, or misproportions the interests supplying the two currents; miscalculation can yield a double disappointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor set-up and stakes to audience expectations: arouse an interest of the appropriate tone and intensity, and proportion the negative and positive elements. Avoid making the negative matter too grave (which kills play) or the positive too trivial (which feels cheap).

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-specific fragility of jokes (not transferable without loss)
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke is not to be mauled, tinkered, or translated about like an old trunk from one nation, race, tribe, language into another; it is a chemical gem, delicate and rooted in the specific; every jest has its season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect cultural, situational, linguistic, and relational specificity. Inside jokes and home-grown familiarities may be powerful locally but fall flat with outsiders. Avoid wholesale transplanting or over-editing of a joke; preserve its precise context and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ridicule/hostility as a common positive motive (but not the whole)
rubrics_metrics.description: One impulse supplying the positive current is hostility or the impulse to fight; ridicule ('sudden glory' or feeling of superiority) often produces laughter and can act as a social corrective, but it is not the sole essence of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ridicule is often the easiest comic effect because human nature supplies the appetite for 'sudden glory.' Use it knowing its power (satire, derision) and danger (cruelty, humiliation). Evaluate whether laughter at someone's debasement is playful or merely harmful; aim for comic rather than merely hostile tones when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexuality as a frequent source of comic energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual impulse is another potent positive current: suppressed carnal hungers supply energy that humor can exploit; many easy jokes rely on insinuated sexual implication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sexual innuendo can reliably provoke laughter, especially where repressed curiosity exists. Cultural taste varies (e.g., Anglo-Saxon furtiveness vs Rabelaisian openness); avoid cheap sniggering or crude implication when aiming for refined humor. Prefer playful, artful handling over mere titillation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth (the appetite for simple truth) as a comic motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond sex and hostility, people are 'always hungry for the simple truth'; truthfulness or exposing plain reality supplies joy-motive in popular jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use revelations of plain, unvarnished truth or comic honesty to satisfy audiences' appetite for truth. This can be combined with the negative/positive mechanics: the truth may function as the gratifying positive element when it cuts through pretension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: laughter from glee vs true humor (tone matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Glee (hysterical whooping at cruelty or obscene quips) is not the same as humor; some loud responses are mere pleasure, not the more discriminating comic feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a laugh derives from coarse glee or from the finer interplay of disappointment and apt satisfaction. For sustained, artistic humor aim for aptness and insight rather than merely provoking high-volume, crude mirth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience maturity: child vs adult modes of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Children laugh indiscriminately at nothing; adults require a hint of real values or delivery for a laugh — children's sense of humor is more primed and violent, adults' is more discriminating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor material to audience maturity. Children's humor tolerates and loves gross, immediate shocks; adult audiences expect a 'point' and some connection to value or insight. When writing for adults, supply the contextual cues that justify laughing at 'nothing.'
